a: Fools they were: for their rebel ways
t: Fools, or he took hold of them?
p: The Hebrew says "fools"; the Greek read "he took hold of them"; many scholars change the word to "sick".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
readings.en: fools, from the way of their rebellion
readings.plain: Fools they were: for their rebel ways

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in the Sixtine edition in Tischendorf, 1877; checked): ἀντελάβετο αὐτῶν ἐξ ὁδοῦ ἀνομίας αὐτῶν
readings.orig: ἀντελάβετο αὐτῶν ἐξ ὁδοῦ ἀνομίας αὐτῶν
readings.en: he took hold of them out of the way of their lawlessness
readings.plain: He took hold of them out of their lawless way;

readings.w: Proposed correction (many commentators): חוֹלִים
readings.en: sick, because of their rebel ways
readings.plain: Sick they were because of their rebel ways

why: No Hebrew manuscript has "sick"; it is a guess that fits the story but smooths away a word that fits the wisdom ending (107:43). The Greek seems to have read a verb, perhaps from a different division of the letters. The Hebrew makes good sense: folly and sin lead to sickness (Proverbs 3:7–8).

a: My heart is firm, God.
t: "My heart is ready" once or twice
p: 57:7 says "my heart is firm" twice. The Hebrew of 108:1 has it once; the Greek has it twice.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: firm is my heart, O God
readings.plain: My heart is firm, God.

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in the Sixtine edition in Tischendorf, 1877; checked): Ἑτοίμη ἡ καρδία μου, ὁ θεός, ἑτοίμη ἡ καρδία μου
readings.orig: Ἑτοίμη ἡ καρδία μου, ὁ θεός, ἑτοίμη ἡ καρδία μου
readings.en: ready is my heart, O God, ready is my heart
readings.plain: My heart is firm, God; my heart is firm.

why: The Hebrew of Psalm 108 is shorter here than 57:7, and it adds "and my glory too" at the end of the line instead. The Greek translator seems to have filled out the line from Psalm 57 (or had a Hebrew copy that did). The Masoretic Text is kept, and the difference from 57:7 is shown in a note.

a: Over Philistia I raise the war cry."
p: The Greek has "foreigners have been made subject to me", as it also does at 60:8.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: over Philistia I will shout in triumph
readings.plain: Over Philistia I raise the war cry."

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in the Sixtine edition in Tischendorf, 1877; checked): ἐμοὶ ἀλλόφυλοι ὑπετάγησαν
readings.en: foreigners have been made subject to me
readings.plain: Foreigners have bowed to me."

why: The Greek calls the Philistines "foreigners" (allophyloi) throughout, and here it gives the sense of the line rather than the war cry. It also reads "Judah my king" and "Moab the cauldron of my hope" in 108:8–9. The Hebrew is kept.

a: let them go searching from their ruins.
p: The Hebrew says they "seek from their ruins"; the Greek has "let them be thrown out of their homes".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and let them seek, from their ruins
readings.plain: let them go searching from their ruins.

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in the Sixtine edition in Tischendorf, 1877; checked): ἐκβληθήτωσαν ἐκ τῶν οἰκοπέδων αὐτῶν
readings.en: let them be thrown out of their dwellings
readings.plain: let them be driven out of their homes.

why: The Greek seems to have read gorshu, "let them be driven out", for dorshu, "let them seek"; only the first letter differs (gimel for dalet). The Hebrew is awkward but makes sense: the sons go begging away from their ruined homes. It is kept.

a: by the next generation let their name be erased.
p: The Hebrew has "in another generation"; the Greek has "in one generation".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: in another generation may their name be wiped out
readings.plain: by the next generation let their name be erased.

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in the Sixtine edition in Tischendorf, 1877; checked): ἐν γενεᾷ μιᾷ ἐξαλειφθείη τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ
readings.orig: ἐν γενεᾷ μιᾷ ἐξαλειφθείη τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ
readings.en: in one generation may his name be wiped out
readings.plain: within one generation let his name be erased.

why: Acher, "another", and echad, "one", differ by one letter, resh and dalet, which are easily confused. The Greek also has "his name" for "their name". Either way the man's line is to die out quickly. The Hebrew is kept.

a: He loved cursing, and it has come home to him;
t: Has come, or let it come?
p: The Hebrew verbs read as past facts; the Greek makes them future; many versions turn them into wishes.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), as pointed (consecutive past)
readings.en: he loved a curse, and it came to him
readings.plain: He loved cursing, and it has come home to him;

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in the Sixtine edition in Tischendorf, 1877; checked): καὶ ἠγάπησε κατάραν, καὶ ἥξει αὐτῷ
readings.orig: καὶ ἠγάπησε κατάραν, καὶ ἥξει αὐτῷ
readings.en: and he loved a curse, and it will come to him
readings.plain: He loved cursing, and it will come home to him;

readings.w: Repointed as wishes (many modern versions)
readings.en: he loved a curse; may it come to him
readings.plain: He loved cursing; let it come home to him;

why: The Masoretic vowels give past tenses: what he loved has already come back on him. Changing one vowel makes a wish, which fits the run of wishes around it, and the Greek has a future. The Hebrew is kept; the sense is close in all three.

a: They have risen up, and they are put to shame,
p: The Greek reads "Let those who rise against me be shamed"; the Hebrew has two past verbs.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: they arose and they were ashamed
readings.plain: They have risen up, and they are put to shame,

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in the Sixtine edition in Tischendorf, 1877; checked): οἱ ἐπανιστάμενοί μοι αἰσχυνθήτωσαν
readings.en: let those who rise against me be put to shame
readings.plain: Let those who rise against me be put to shame,

why: The Greek translator read the line as a wish, like the lines around it; many scholars think its Hebrew had qamai, "those who rise against me". The Masoretic Text, which describes the shame as already happening, is kept.

a: Your people are freewill offerings
t: "Your people are willing" or "With you is rule"
p: The Hebrew has "your people, freewill offerings"; the Greek has "with you is rule".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: your people are freewill offerings
readings.plain: Your people are freewill offerings

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in the Sixtine edition in Tischendorf, 1877; checked): μετὰ σοῦ ἡ ἀρχὴ
readings.en: with you is the rule (or the beginning)
readings.plain: With you is royal rule

why: The Greek read the same consonants 'mk as 'immekha, "with you", instead of 'ammekha, "your people", and took ndbt as "nobility", "princely rule" (compare nadiv, "noble"). The Latin Tecum principium follows the Greek. The Masoretic reading fits the next line, about the day the king calls up his army, and is kept.

a: In holy splendor, out of the dawn's womb,
p: The Leningrad Codex reads "in the splendors of holiness"; many Hebrew manuscripts and Jerome read "on the holy mountains".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: in splendors of holiness
readings.plain: In holy splendor, out of the dawn's womb,

readings.w: Many Hebrew manuscripts; Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew (in montibus sanctis) and Symmachus, as reported
readings.en: on mountains of holiness
readings.plain: On the holy mountains, out of the dawn's womb,

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs): ἐν ταῖς λαμπρότησιν τῶν ἁγίων
readings.en: in the splendors of the holy ones
readings.plain: In the splendor of the holy ones, out of the womb,

why: Hadrei, "splendors", and harerei, "mountains", differ by one letter, dalet and resh. "Holy mountains" fits Zion (87:1; 2:6), and many scholars prefer it. "Holy splendor" is the phrase of 29:2 and 96:9, perhaps sacred robes. The Greek read the Hebrew as "holy ones"; Codex Vaticanus, as printed in the Sixtine edition, adds "your". The Leningrad reading is kept. The Hebrew manuscripts and Jerome are reported by Allen and the standard apparatus.

a: the dew of your young years is yours.
p: The Greek reads "from the womb, before the morning star, I fathered you", taking the same consonants differently.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: from the womb of the dawn, to you is the dew of your youth
readings.plain: the dew of your young years is yours.

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in the Sixtine edition in Tischendorf, 1877; checked): ἐκ γαστρὸς πρὸ ἑωσφόρου ἐγέννησά σε
readings.orig: ἐκ γαστρὸς πρὸ ἑωσφόρου ἐγέννησά σε
readings.en: from the womb, before the morning star, I fathered you
readings.plain: I have fathered you.

why: The Greek read yelidtikha, "I have fathered you", for yaldutekha, "your youth", with the same consonants and other vowels (as in 2:7, yelidtikha); some Hebrew manuscripts are pointed that way too. It read mishchar as "before the dawn" and seems not to have had tal, "dew". The Sixtine text prints egennēsa; Rahlfs' edition prints exegennēsa, with the same sense. The Masoretic Text is kept; the Greek reading and its long Christian history are explained in the notes.
b: The Greek is the root of the church's use of this verse for the eternal birth of the Son (see the note on 110:3). Jewish readers follow the Hebrew vowels. Modern translations divide: most follow the Masoretic Text, a few print "I have begotten you" from the Greek and from some Hebrew manuscripts.

a: Praise the LORD!
p: The Greek has no closing Hallelujah here and puts it at the head of Psalm 114 instead.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: praise Yah
readings.plain: Praise the LORD!

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in the Sixtine edition in Tischendorf, 1877; checked): no Ἀλληλούϊα at the end; Psalm 114 (Greek 113) opens with Ἀλληλούϊα
readings.en: (nothing)

why: In Codex Vaticanus (Sixtine text) "Alleluia" is a heading at the start of a psalm, not a closing shout. So the closing Hallelujahs of 106:48, 113:9, 115:18, 116:19 and 117:2 stand instead at the head of Psalms 107, 114, 116, 117 and 118 (Greek 106, 113, 114, 116 and 117), and 106 ends with "So be it, so be it." Greek 115 (Hebrew 116:10) and Greek 118 (Hebrew 119) also open with Alleluia, where the Hebrew has none. 111, 112 and 113 open with it in both. The Masoretic placement is kept. Either way, the word marks the psalms as songs of praise.

a: Israel, put your trust in the LORD!
p: The Hebrew is a command, "Trust!" The Greek has "The house of Israel has hoped in the Lord."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: Israel, trust in the LORD
readings.plain: Israel, put your trust in the LORD!

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in the Sixtine edition in Tischendorf, 1877; checked): οἶκος Ἰσραὴλ ἤλπισεν ἐπὶ κύριον
readings.en: the house of Israel has hoped in the Lord
readings.plain: The house of Israel has put its hope in the LORD;

why: The Greek read batach, "he trusted", for betach, "trust!", with the same consonants, and so in 115:10–11. It also adds "house of" from 115:12. The Hebrew commands fit the change to "their help" in the second line, which sounds like a response. They are kept.

a: I kept trusting, even when I said,
p: The Hebrew is hard. The Greek, quoted by Paul, has "I believed; therefore I spoke."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: I believed, for (or when) I speak
readings.plain: I kept trusting, even when I said,

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in the Sixtine edition in Tischendorf, 1877; checked): Ἐπίστευσα, διὸ ἐλάλησα
readings.en: I believed; therefore I spoke
readings.plain: I believed; therefore I spoke:

why: The Hebrew ki can mean "for", "when" or "even though"; the Greek dio, "therefore", is an interpretation, not a different text. The Greek also starts a new psalm here (Greek 115). Paul quotes the Greek in 2 Corinthians 4:13. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew and reads ki as "even when", since what he said next was a cry of distress (116:10b–11).

a: Sheltering in the LORD is better
p: Two Qumran scrolls read "to trust in the LORD" where the Masoretic Text has "to take shelter".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: better to take refuge in the LORD
readings.plain: Sheltering in the LORD is better

readings.w: Qumran: 4QPs-b (4Q84) and 11QPs-a (11Q5), transcription of Abegg, Bowley and Cook (ETCBC dss dataset); checked
readings.en: better to trust in the LORD
readings.plain: Trusting in the LORD is better

why: The scrolls use the same verb, batach, in both halves of the line, so that it reads "better to trust in the LORD than to trust in people". The Masoretic Text varies the verbs, "take shelter" and "rely", as it does again in 118:9, where both scrolls agree with it. The scrolls' reading looks like a leveling of the two halves, so the Masoretic Text is kept.

a: than relying on nobles.
p: 11QPs-a adds a line: "better to trust in the LORD than to trust in a thousand people".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QPs-b (4Q84)
readings.en: than to trust in nobles
readings.plain: than relying on nobles.

readings.w: 11QPs-a (11Q5), in its group of Psalm 118 verses after Psalm 136, transcription of Abegg, Bowley and Cook (ETCBC dss dataset); checked
readings.orig: מבטוח בנדיבים טוב לבטוח ביהוה מבטוח באלף עם
readings.en: than to trust in nobles; better to trust in the LORD than to trust in a thousand people
readings.plain: than relying on nobles. / Trusting in the LORD is better / than relying on a thousand people.

why: The extra line comes in 11QPs-a's short gathering of Psalm 118 verses (118:1, 15, 16, 8, 9, 29) that follows Psalm 136. It repeats the pattern of 118:8–9 with a new contrast, and seems to be a liturgical expansion. 4QPs-b and the other witnesses have the shorter verse, which is kept.

a: They closed in, they closed in all around me;
p: The Qumran scroll 4QPs-b goes straight from 118:10 to 118:12 and has no 118:11.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Old Greek
readings.en: they surrounded me, yes, they surrounded me
readings.plain: They closed in, they closed in all around me;

readings.w: 4QPs-b (4Q84), transcription of Abegg, Bowley and Cook (ETCBC dss dataset); checked
readings.en: (the verse is absent)

why: The three lines of 118:10–12 all end "in the LORD's name I cut them down", so a copyist's eye could easily jump from the end of 118:10 to the end of 118:11 and drop a whole verse. 4QPs-b also has other gaps and differences. The Masoretic Text, with its threefold refrain, is kept; the Old Greek has the verse too.

a: they flickered out like a fire in thornbushes;
p: The Hebrew says the enemies "were put out" like a thorn fire; the Greek says they "blazed up" like one.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: they were extinguished like a fire of thorns
readings.plain: they flickered out like a fire in thornbushes;

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in the Sixtine edition in Tischendorf, 1877; checked): ἐξεκαύθησαν ὡς πῦρ ἐν ἀκάνθαις
readings.en: they blazed up like fire among thorns
readings.plain: they blazed up like fire among thorns;

why: The Greek may have read ba'aru, "they burned", or simply guessed at the rare verb do'akhu. The Greek also adds that the bees swarm around "a honeycomb". The Hebrew fits the point of the picture, a fire that dies as fast as it starts, and is kept.

a: You shoved me, shoved me, to make me fall,
p: The Hebrew speaks to the enemy: "you pushed me". The Greek and many versions have "I was pushed".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: you pushed me hard to fall
readings.plain: You shoved me, shoved me, to make me fall,

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in the Sixtine edition in Tischendorf, 1877; checked): ὠσθεὶς ἀνετράπην τοῦ πεσεῖν
readings.en: pushed, I was overturned so as to fall
readings.plain: I was pushed hard and overturned, about to fall,

why: The Greek and the Syriac read a passive, nidcheti, "I was pushed". The Hebrew turns suddenly to address the enemy, or the hostile nations as one, which is harsh but possible in poetry. The Masoretic Text is kept. The Syriac is reported, not checked.

a: the right hand of the LORD acts with might!"
t: "Acts with might" or "has done a mighty deed"
p: 11QPs-a ends 118:16 with "has done a mighty deed" (gevurah) for the Masoretic "acts with might" (chayil).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: the right hand of the LORD does valor
readings.plain: the right hand of the LORD acts with might!"

readings.w: 11QPs-a (11Q5), in its group of Psalm 118 verses after Psalm 136, transcription of Abegg, Bowley and Cook (ETCBC dss dataset); checked
readings.en: the right hand of the LORD has done a mighty deed
readings.plain: the right hand of the LORD has done a mighty deed!"

why: The scroll varies the repeated line with a synonym. The Masoretic Text repeats 118:15's wording exactly, which suits the refrain, and is kept.

a: Tie the festival offering with cords
t: Tie the offering, or arrange the festival?
p: The Greek has "arrange a festival with thick boughs, up to the horns of the altar".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: bind the festival with cords
readings.plain: Tie the festival offering with cords

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in the Sixtine edition in Tischendorf, 1877; checked): συστήσασθε ἑορτὴν ἐν τοῖς πυκάζουσιν
readings.en: set up a festival with thick-leaved branches
readings.plain: Arrange the festival with leafy boughs

why: The Greek read the same Hebrew but took 'avotim as leafy branches (as in Ezekiel 19:11) and chag as the festival itself, which fits the Booths procession with branches. The Hebrew can bear that meaning too (see the note). The Plain English Translation keeps the plainer sense of the words, an offering tied with cords.

a: my God, I will lift you high.
t: A longer ending in the Greek
p: After 118:28 the Greek repeats 118:21: "I will thank you, for you answered me and became my rescue."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: my God, I will exalt you
readings.plain: my God, I will lift you high.

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Codex Vaticanus, as printed in the Sixtine edition in Tischendorf, 1877; checked): adds ἐξομολογήσομαί σοι, ὅτι ἐπήκουσάς μου καὶ ἐγένου μοι εἰς σωτηρίαν
readings.orig: ἐξομολογήσομαί σοι, ὅτι ἐπήκουσάς μου καὶ ἐγένου μοι εἰς σωτηρίαν
readings.en: my God, I will exalt you. I will thank you, for you answered me and became my rescue
readings.plain: my God, I will lift you high. / I will thank you, for you answered me / and became my rescue.

why: The extra lines repeat 118:21 exactly and seem to be a liturgical echo added to round off the psalm before the closing refrain. The shorter Hebrew is kept.
